title: FinTech, Lesson 5: Fraud and chargebacks - the cost nobody puts in the forecast
subtitle: How payment fraud eats into margin, and why over-tightening costs more than the losses themselves
whyItMatters: With a take rate below 1%, a fraud rate of just 0.3% wipes out a third of the margin. This is the only cost in fintech where controlling too loosely and controlling too tightly both do damage, which means it has to be managed rather than eliminated.
openingQuestion: A platform has a take rate of 0.8% and a fraud rate of 0.2% of volume. What share of the margin does fraud consume?
openingOptions: Negligible, since 0.2% is a very small number
Cannot be computed without knowing the average number of transactions per day
explanation: Fraud eats into volume, while revenue is only a thin slice of that volume - so the two numbers have to be compared on the same denominator. 0.2% divided by 0.8% is 25%: a quarter of the margin disappears. This is what makes fraud an existential problem in payments and not in ordinary retail: a shop on a 30% margin losing 0.2% of sales loses less than one percent of its profit, while a payment platform loses a quarter. Same rate, consequences dozens of times apart, purely because the margin is thin.

diagram.label: The cardholder disputes it with the bank
Chargeback: the money is clawed back
The platform bears the loss + the handling fee + the risk of being put under monitoring

realWorldExample.company: The Visa and Mastercard chargeback thresholds
realWorldExample.description: Both card networks set a chargeback rate threshold, typically around 0.9% of transactions. Cross it and the merchant is placed into a monitoring programme, charged a penalty per transaction, and can have the connection cut off. Which means fraud does not only cost the money lost - it can cost the right to operate at all.

quiz.question: What is a chargeback?
options: A penalty fee charged on a transaction flagged as suspicious
A transaction clawed back after the cardholder disputes it
A refund the platform voluntarily pays the customer to keep them
A provision set aside against transactions showing unusual patterns
quiz.explanation: A chargeback is the process by which a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank and the money is taken back from the receiving side. The merchant bears both the loss and the handling fee. It is not a voluntary refund - the merchant does not choose it - and it is not an accounting provision either: it is a real cash reversal that has already happened.

quiz.question: Why is fraud more dangerous in payments than in ordinary retail?
options: Because Vietnamese law requires the payment platform to compensate double the transaction value
Because payment transactions cannot be traced once they have been completed
Because payment margins are thin, so the same loss rate eats a far larger share of profit
Because customers of a payment platform complain more than retail customers do
quiz.explanation: Losing 0.2% of volume when the take rate is 0.8% means losing a quarter of the margin. A retailer on a 30% margin losing the same rate barely notices it. Payment transactions are in fact highly traceable, no law imposes double compensation, and complaint frequency is not the mechanism - it is arithmetic about the size of the slice, not about behaviour.

quiz.question: What damage does over-tightening fraud controls cause?
options: It stretches transaction processing time past the limit the card networks allow
It raises server infrastructure costs beyond the losses it manages to prevent
It breaches the regulations on protecting users' personal data
It blocks genuine transactions, losing revenue and losing customers
quiz.explanation: The false positive rate is a real cost and is usually larger than the fraud it prevents. A customer wrongly declined rarely tries a second time, so the loss continues rather than ending with that one transaction. Processing latency, infrastructure cost and data protection are all real constraints on a fraud system, but none of them is the expensive one - the lost genuine customers are.

quiz.question: What is the optimal level of fraud for a platform?
options: The level at which the cost of blocking one more unit of fraud starts to exceed that unit
Zero - every transaction that looks suspicious should simply be blocked outright
Exactly the chargeback threshold laid down by the card networks themselves
The average level reported by other platforms of a comparable size
quiz.explanation: This is a marginal problem. Driving fraud to zero requires tightening to the point of blocking large numbers of genuine transactions, and the revenue lost exceeds the amount saved. The network threshold is a ceiling you must stay under, not a target to aim at, and the peer average tells you nothing about your own cost curve.

quiz.question: What is the most serious consequence of breaching the card networks' chargeback threshold?
options: Being forced to refund every single fee collected from customers during the period
Being placed under monitoring, fined, and possibly losing the payment connection
Being downgraded on credit and paying more to borrow from banks
Being required to raise charter capital under the regulator's rules
quiz.explanation: Losing the connection is the worst outcome because it ends the business rather than merely reducing profit. That is why fraud management belongs in the survival risk category rather than the cost category. A credit downgrade or a capital requirement would hurt, but the company would still be able to process payments the following morning.

practicePrompt.question: After tightening the blocking thresholds, fraud losses fall from 12bn to 5bn a year, but wrongly blocked orders cost 19bn of lost revenue. What is the conclusion?
options: Over-tightened: 7bn saved but 19bn lost
The right direction, since fraud more than halved
Tighten further until fraud is near zero
Not comparable, as the two amounts differ in nature
practicePrompt.explanation: A false decline is a real cost; it just has no invoice attached and nobody inside the company has to explain it, whereas every fraud case comes with a specific number somebody has to report. That asymmetry is why almost every control team over-tightens. Here the amount saved is 7bn and the extra amount lost is 19bn, so this tightening step is a net loss of 12bn. The goal is not zero fraud but the point where the last marginal unit spent on blocking exactly equals the loss it prevents.

keyTakeaways: Fraud eats into volume while revenue is only a thin slice of volume - compare them on the same denominator to see the real damage.
A chargeback takes both the money and the handling fee, and breaching the threshold takes the connection itself.
False declines are a real cost, usually larger than the fraud they prevent.
The goal is not zero fraud, but the marginal cost optimum.

summary.keyIdea: The goal is not zero fraud, but the marginal cost optimum
summary.commonMistake: Comparing fraud losses against revenue instead of against transaction volume, which makes the number look many times smaller than it is.
summary.action: Estimate both sides: money lost to fraud, and revenue lost to genuine transactions wrongly blocked.

application.title: Find the point of over-tightening
application.message: For any fraud blocking rule, ask how much fraud it stops and how many genuine transactions it costs. If the second number is bigger, that rule is running at a loss.
application.secondary: False declines appear in no loss report anywhere, which is why they are almost always left out of the calculation.

sections.text: In every forecasting model for a payment product there is one line that is almost always left blank in the first draft: the money that will be lost to fraud. It is never zero, and on a thin margin it is never small.
Why a small number takes a large bite

Fraud is measured against transaction volume, while revenue is only the take rate multiplied by that volume. With a take rate of 0.8% and fraud of 0.2%, a quarter of the margin disappears. The same rate at a retailer on a 30% margin would go almost unnoticed.

left.label: Too loose
left.text: Fraud gets through, chargebacks rise, penalty fees rise, and if the card network threshold is breached the connection goes.

right.label: Too tight
right.text: Genuine transactions get blocked. A customer wrongly declined rarely comes back, so this loss persists rather than ending after one attempt.

items: Measure the fraud rate against volume, not against transaction count - one large transaction equals hundreds of small ones.
Measure the false decline rate too, otherwise every improvement will run in one direction only: tighter.
Track the chargeback rate against the card networks' threshold, because that is a survival threshold rather than a cost threshold.
Put fraud cost into the product's contribution margin from the very first version of the forecast.

sections.label: How to set the target correctly
sections.text: Do not set a target of 'reduce fraud to zero'. Set it at the level where the cost of blocking one more unit of fraud starts to exceed that unit itself - everything below that line is a loss cheaper than the spending required to avoid it.

lines: Fraud is a cost of doing business, not an incident.
A product whose model does not have that line in it is a model that is not finished.
